through_line: Who gets to say yes. The team is designing approvals for agent actions, and the reads disagree on how. One argues people stop reading approval prompts by the third click. Step-up auth asks for fresh proof only on the risky action. And Claude's new 1,000-agent workflows apply permission checks to the tools each agent calls, but not to starting the run.

items.title: What happens when a dbt run fails at incident.io
items.summary: Step three: the real world, and how it fails. Our own data team runs dbt hourly on CircleCI, and a failed model or test fires an HTTP alert that opens an incident. A weekly Data Responder owns it, test warnings included. The useful part is the routing: the same dbt run powers customer-facing Insights, so overnight failures with customer impact page engineering, while internal ones wait for working hours.

items.title: How a pentester turned an 'informational' finding into server takeover
items.summary: Step three: how it actually works, through one real engagement. Three apps share a hostname on different ports, so they share cookies. One app's session cookie lacks HttpOnly, another has reflected XSS, and a third needs admin for a file-upload RCE. The tester chains them, with a 5-second setTimeout as the trick that finally worked. You'll see why reports rate chains, not single bugs, and why scanners miss them.

items.title: Why the 'approve this action?' button fails as a safety control
items.summary: A security lead argues that approval prompts for agent actions decay into reflex. Microsoft found Vista users approved 89% of UAC prompts, and 47% of Chrome users who clicked through a certificate warning did so within 1.5 seconds. His answer is to scope what an agent can reach rather than ask a human at every step. It's long, but each section stands alone, so the first three are enough for one ride.

also.title: HITL approvals compared: tool approval, durable execution, wait-for-event

items.title: Making users prove it's still them before a dangerous action
items.summary: A login from eight hours ago shouldn't let someone revoke API keys. This walks through the mechanics: an auth_time claim on the token, an OIDC max_age parameter that forces fresh verification, and a session ID that survives the re-auth. GitHub's 'sudo mode' post is the original, shorter take on the same pattern.

items.title: Claude can now start runs of up to 1,000 agents by itself
items.summary: With dynamic workflows, a lead agent writes a program that runs worker agents in phases and merges what they find. In Anthropic's bug-hunt test, one agent found 27 of 70 seeded bugs and the swarm found 66. Read it for the operational fine print: permission policies cover the tools workers call but not the decision to start a run, the budget can overshoot by one request per thread, and 64 threads run at once.

items.title: Meta swaps Instagram Live's video transport without anyone noticing
items.summary: Instagram Live ingest now runs on MoQ, an IETF protocol built on QUIC where relays cache and fan out media without parsing it. Most of the post is a migration playbook. A shim at the edge translates MoQ into the old protocol so nothing downstream changes, server-side routing lets them resize the rollout in minutes, and the TCP fallback copes with networks that block UDP. The target was parity, and they hit it.

items.title: Meta turns idle GPUs into optional work it can drop in milliseconds
items.summary: An inference fleet can be short of capacity overall while pockets of it sit idle. Meta runs optional work in that slack: ranking more candidates and sending some requests to a bigger model. A PID controller keyed on tail latency sets how much optional work to accept, and value-aware load shedding on both client and server covers the minutes before the controller catches up.

items.title: Passing memory between agents as KV cache instead of text
items.summary: Sunday's AlphaSignal deep dive covered handing an agent's KV cache to another model instead of re-reading everything, which cut a 32k-token handoff from about 7 seconds to 278ms. Ramp's write-up is the hands-on version. It compacts the orchestrator's KV cache down to what the worker's task attends to, saving 42-57% of worker tokens at slightly higher accuracy. The SwarmKV post is a funny practitioner build of 'prefill once, fan out'.

also.title: Prefill Once, Fan Out: KV snapshot sharing for multi-agent pipelines

items.title: Marc Brooker: formal methods make you faster, not slower
items.summary: Brooker, an AWS engineer, makes the economic case: software lets you start building before the design is done, so design mistakes turn into rewrites, and Hyrum's Law makes shipped behaviour expensive to change. He's specific about where it pays off (distributed and low-level systems) and where it doesn't (UIs and pricing logic). The best line is from an AWS team whose TLA+ spec 'verified an aggressive optimization'.
